# Reactions of the Halide Ions ## Halide Ions: Reducing Agents > **Spec point** — `spcpt_kYX8rJ8Ff8TSC2TK` ## Halide Ions: Reducing Agents - Halide ions can also act as **reducing agents **and donate electrons to another atom - The halide ions themselves get **oxidised** and lose electrons - The **reducing power **of the halide ions **increases **going down the group - This trend can be explained by looking at the ionic radii of the halides’ ions #### The ionic radii of the halide ions ![Diagram showing electron configurations of halide ions: fluoride, chloride, bromide, and iodide, with increasing electron shells from left to right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/e65c0a44c206-2-3-group-17-electron-arrangement-in-halide-ions.png) *The diagram shows that going down the group the ionic radii of the halogens increases* - Going down the group, the halide ions become **larger** - The outermost electrons get further away from the nucleus - The outermost electrons also experience more **shielding** by inner electrons - As a result of this, the outermost electrons are held **less** **tightly** to the positively charged nucleus - Therefore, the halide ions lose electrons more easily going down the group and their **reducing power **increases #### Linking the ionic radius to the reducing power of the halide ions ![Diagram showing ionic radii of F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ ions, with labelled vertical arrow indicating smallest ionic radius at top to strongest reducing agent at bottom.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/429921138d98-group-17-reducing-power-trend-downloadable-as-an.png) *The reducing power of the halide ions increases going down the group* > **Exam Hint** > The **ionic radius** is a measure of the size of an atom’s **ion** ## Reactions of Halide Ions > **Spec point** — `spcpt_zZKJqYbTPGy3vBTg` ## Reactions of Halide Ions ### Silver ions & ammonia - Halide ions can be identified in an **unknown** **solution** by dissolving the solution in **nitric acid **and then adding a **silver nitrate solution **followed by **ammonia **solution - The halide ions will react with the silver nitrate solution as follows: **General equation: AgNO****3 ****(aq) + X****– ****(aq) → AgX (s) + NO****3****–**** ****(aq)** **Ionic equation: Ag****+ ****(aq) + X****– ****(aq) → AgX (s)** - **X****-** is the halide ion in both equations - If the unknown solution contains halide ions, then a **precipitate** of the **silver halide** will be formed (AgX) #### Testing for halide ions 1. Add the halide solution to a clean test tube using a pipette 2. Add a few drops of **nitric acid** 3. Add a few drops of **silver nitrate solution** ![Test tubes show a reaction where silver nitrate is added to an unknown halide solution in dilute nitric acid, forming a silver halide precipitate.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/042a586f831c-2-3-group-17-halide-test.png) *A silver halide precipitate is formed upon the addition of silver nitrate solution to halide ion solution* 4. Observe the formation of a coloured precipitate: ![Three test tubes with blue liquid show different precipitates: left has white, middle has cream, and right has yellow. Labels indicate precipitate colours.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/48766056df32-41362-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads20250627149.png) *The white, cream and yellow precipitates formed when halide ions react with silver nitrate solution* - Each precipitate is associated with a specific halide ion: - A white precipitate of AgCl forms if chloride ions are present - A cream precipitate of AgBr forms if bromide ions are present - A yellow precipitate of AgI forms if iodide ions are present #### Adding ammonia after the halide ion test - The silver halide precipitates can look similar - So, an additional test using ammonia solution can confirm their identity 1. Add **dilute ammonia** solution dropwise to the silver halide precipitate - If the precipitate dissolves, the halide is **chloride** (AgCl) ![Two test tubes: left with white AgCl precipitate, label states "AgCl precipitate"; right empty, label states "AgCl forms soluble complex with dilute ammonia".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/9375389f7972-37856-agcl-precipitate.png) 2. If the precipitate does not dissolve, add **concentrated ammonia** - If the precipitate now dissolves, the halide is **bromide** (AgBr) ![Two test tubes: on the left a cream precipitate of AgBr; on the right a clear colourless solution after the precipitate has dissolved in concentrated ammonia, forming a soluble complex.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/ebf981299a4f-agbr-precipitate.png) - If the precipitate still does not dissolve, the halide is **iodide** (AgI) ![Test tubes with yellow AgI precipitate, one labelled "AgI PRECiPITATE," highlighting it doesn't form a soluble complex with ammonia.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/864119aba6ee-41378-agi-precipitate.png) #### Reaction of halide ions with silver nitrate & ammonia solutions table | **Halide ion** | **Colour of silver halide precipitate** | **Effect of adding dilute ammonia solution to the precipitate** | **Effect of adding concentrated ammonia solution to the precipitate** | |---|---|---|---| | **Cl****–**** (aq)** | White | Dissolves | Dissolves | | **Br****–**** (aq)** | Cream | Insoluble | Dissolves | | **I****–**** (aq)** | Yellow | Insoluble | Insoluble | ### Concentrated sulfuric acid - Chloride, bromide and iodide ions react with concentrated sulfuric acid to produce **toxic gases** - These reactions should therefore be carried out in a fume cupboard - The general reaction of the halide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid is: **General equation: H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) + X****– ****(aq) → HX (g) + HSO****4****– ****(aq)** - Where **X****–** is the halide ion ### Reaction of chloride ions with concentrated sulfuric acid - Concentrated sulfuric acid is dropwise added to sodium chloride crystals to produce **hydrogen chloride gas** - The hydrogen chloride gas produced is **wet**, so it can be passed through a conical flask of concentrated sulfuric acid to produce **dry** hydrogen chloride gas #### Apparatus for the reaction of sodium chloride with concentrated sulfuric acid ![Diagram showing the production of dry HCl gas. HCl is formed by heating NaCl with H2SO4, dried and collected in a gas jar.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/f1a799143abd-nacl-and-h2so4-experiment.png) *Sodium chloride reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form dense hydrogen chloride gas* - The reaction that takes place is: **H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) + NaCl (s) → HCl (g) + NaHSO****4 ****(s) ** - The HCl gas produced is seen as **white fumes** ### Reaction of bromide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid - The **thermal stability **of the hydrogen halides decreases down the group - The reaction of sodium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid is: **H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) + NaBr (s) → HBr (g) + NaHSO****4 ****(s) ** - The concentrated sulfuric acid **oxidises **HBr to **bromine**, and the sulfuric acid itself is **reduced **to **sulfur** **dioxide** **gas** (water is also formed): **2HBr (g) + H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) → Br****2 ****(g) + SO****2 ****(g) + 2H****2****O (l)** - The bromine is seen as a **reddish-brown gas** ### Reaction of iodide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid - The reaction of sodium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid is: **H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) + NaI (s) → HI (g) + NaHSO****4 ****(s) ** - **Hydrogen iodide **decomposes the **easiest** - Sulfuric acid oxidises the hydrogen iodide to several extents: - The concentrated sulfuric acid **oxidises **HI and is itself **reduced **to **sulfur** **dioxide** **gas**: **2HI (g) + H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) → I****2 ****(g) + SO****2 ****(g) + 2H****2****O (l)** - Iodine is seen as a violet/purple vapour - The concentrated sulfuric acid **oxidises **HI and is itself **reduced **to **sulfur**: **6HI (g) + H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) → 3I****2 ****(g) + S (s) + 4H****2****O (l)** - Sulfur is seen as a **yellow solid** - The concentrated sulfuric acid **oxidises **HI and is itself **reduced **to **hydrogen sulfide**: **8HI (g) + H****2****SO****4 ****(aq) → 4I****2 ****(g) + H****2****S (g) + 4H****2****O (l)** - Hydrogen sulfide has a **strong smell of bad eggs** #### Halide ion reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid table | **Halide ion** | **Reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid** | **Observations** | |---|---|---| | **Cl****–**** (aq)** | H2SO4 (aq) + NaCl (s) → HCl (g) + NaHSO4 (aq) | White fumes of HCl gas | | **Br****–**** (aq)** | H2SO4 (aq) + NaBr (s) → HBr (g) + NaHSO4 (s)

2HBr (g) + H2SO4 (aq) → Br2 (g) + SO2 (g) + 2H2O (l) | Reddish brown Br2 gas | | **I****–**** (aq)** | H2SO4 (aq) + NaI (s) → HI (g) + NaHSO4 (s)

H2SO4 (aq) + 2HI (g) → I2 (g) + SO2 (g) + 2H2O (l)

H2SO4 (aq) + 6HI (g) → 3I2 (g) + S (s) + 4H2O (l)

H2SO4 (aq) + 8HI (g) → 4I2 (g) + H2S (g) + 4H2O (l) | Violet / purple I2 vapour

Yellow solid of S

Strong, bad (egg) smell of H2S | > **Exam Hint** > It gets easier to oxidise the hydrogen halides as you descend Group 17: the halides become stronger **reducing agents**

title: The Reactions of Chlorine
bodyMd:
# The Reactions of Chlorine

## Reaction of Chlorine

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_jGFrWZDkRVsdCjCm`

## Reaction of Chlorine

- A **disproportionation** **reaction** is a reaction in which the same species is both oxidised and reduced
- The reaction of **chlorine **with **dilute alkali** is an example of a disproportionation reaction
- In these reactions, the chlorine gets oxidised and reduced at the same time
- Different reactions take place at different **temperatures **of the dilute alkali

### Chlorine in cold alkali (15 <sup>o</sup>C)

- The reaction that takes place is:

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaCl (aq) + NaClO (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The ionic equation is:

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 2OH**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) → Cl**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + ClO**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The ionic equations show that the chlorine undergoes disproportionation, i.e. gets both oxidised and reduced
- Chlorine gets oxidised as there is an increase in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to +1 in ClO<sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The half-equation for the oxidation reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 2OH**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) → ClO**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + e**<sup>**–**</sup>

- Chlorine gets reduced as there is a decrease in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to –1 in Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The half-equation for the reduction reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + e**<sup>**–**</sup>** → Cl**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

### Chlorine in hot alkali (70 <sup>o</sup>C)

- The reaction that takes place is:

**3Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO**<sub>**3**</sub>** (aq) + 3H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The ionic equation is:

**3Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 6OH**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) → 5Cl**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + ClO**<sub>**3**</sub><sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + 3H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l)**

- The ionic equations show that the chlorine undergoes disproportionation, i.e. gets both oxidised and reduced
- Chlorine gets oxidised as there is an increase in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to +5 in ClO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The half-equation for the oxidation reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + 6OH**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) → ClO**<sub>**3**</sub><sup>**–**</sup>** (aq) + 3H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + 5e**<sup>**–**</sup>

- Chlorine gets reduced as there is a decrease in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to –1 in Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The simplified half-equation for the reduction reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + e**<sup>**–**</sup>** → Cl**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

## Chlorine in Water Purification

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_CrBkTRVmDxRCscQ4`

## Chlorine in Water Purification

- Chlorine can be used to clean water and make it drinkable
- The reaction of chlorine in water is a **disproportionation reaction **in which the chlorine gets both **oxidised **and **reduced**

**Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌ HCl (aq) + HClO (aq)**

- The ionic equations show that the chlorine undergoes disproportionation, i.e. gets both oxidised and reduced
- Chlorine gets oxidised as there is an increase in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to +1 in ClO<sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The half-equation for the oxidation reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) → HClO (aq) + H**<sup>**+**</sup>** (aq) + e**<sup>**–**</sup>

- Chlorine gets reduced as there is a decrease in oxidation number from 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> (aq) to –1 in Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

  - The half-equation for the reduction reaction is:

**½Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (aq) + e**<sup>**–**</sup>** → Cl**<sup>**–**</sup>** (aq)**

- Chloric(I) acid (HClO) **sterilises **water by killing **bacteria**
- Chloric(I) acid is a weak acid and partially dissociates in water to form ClO<sup>- </sup>(aq):

**HClO (aq) ⇌ H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + ClO**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- ClO<sup>-</sup>(aq) also acts as a **sterilising agent **cleaning the water

> **Exam Hint**
> Adding chlorine to a water supply is an effective way to make the water safe to drink as it forms the sterilising agent HClO which in turn dissociates in water into another sterilising agent, ClO<sup>– </sup>(aq)

title: Nitrogen & its Compounds
bodyMd:
# Nitrogen & its Compounds

## Reactivity of Nitrogen

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_ZjJ8YTCQ7qJK2VKm`

## Reactivity of Nitrogen

- Nitrogen is a **diatomic **molecule and the main **unreactive gas** in air
- 78% of air is nitrogen gas
- The lack of reactivity of nitrogen gas can be explained by looking at its **intramolecular bonds**
- Intramolecular bonds are the bonds **within **a molecule

### Bonding in nitrogen

- The electron configuration of a nitrogen atom is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>3</sup>
- To achieve a full outer shell of electrons, it needs to gain three electrons
- Nitrogen atoms therefore form a **triple covalent bond** between two nitrogen atoms in which they **share **three electrons with each other

#### Bonding in nitrogen

![Diagram of nitrogen atoms forming a nitrogen molecule. Two N atoms with electrons shown as circles, forming triple bonds in N₂. Configuration (2,8).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/cdb26803d006-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-bonding-in-nitrogen-1.png)

*The diagram shows a triple covalent bond between two nitrogen atoms to achieve a full outer shell of electrons*

- The **bond energy **of the nitrogen triple bond is 944 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
- This means that 1000 kJ of energy is needed to break one mole of N<sub>2</sub> triple bond
- As it is so difficult to break the nitrogen triple bond, nitrogen and oxygen gas in air will not react with each other
- Only under extreme conditions will nitrogen gas react (e.g. during a thunderstorm)

### Polarity of nitrogen

- The electrons in a nitrogen molecule are shared **equally** between the two nitrogen atoms
- Therefore, nitrogen molecules are **nonpolar** molecules

#### Polarity in a nitrogen bond

![Diagram of a nitrogen molecule with a triple bond, represented by two overlapping purple spheres and a structural formula. Red arrows indicate bond length.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/b7f76e306dd9-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-polarity-nitrogen.png)

*Since the electronegativity of the two nitrogen atoms is the same, the will pull the electrons towards them equally so overall the molecule is nonpolar*

- Due to the lack of polarity, nitrogen gas is **not attracted to** or **likely to react with** other molecules the way polar molecules would

> **Exam Hint**
> Nitrogen is very unreactive due to the lack of polarity and strength of its triple bond.

## Properties of Ammonia

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_yVqXHvZMbCYqrTPB`

## Properties of Ammonia

- **Ammonia** is a compound of nitrogen and will turn damp** red **litmus paper** blue** as it is an **alkaline** gas
- Ammonia is made on a large scale in industry using the **Haber **process:

**N**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + 3H**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) ⇌ 2NH**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(g)**

### Basicity of ammonia

- Ammonia can act as a **Brønsted–Lowry base** by accepting a **proton** (H<sup>+</sup>) using the **lone** **pair** of electrons on the nitrogen atom to form an **ammonium ion**:

**NH**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(aq) + H**<sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) →  NH**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq)**

- In an aqueous solution of ammonia, an equilibrium mixture is established

**NH**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌  NH**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + OH**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- Since the position of the equilibrium lies well over to the left the ammonia solution is only **weakly alkaline**
- There is a higher concentration of ammonia molecules than hydroxide ions in solution
- Ammonia is therefore a **weak base**

### Structure & formation of ammonium ion

- The ammonium ion is formed by an acid-base reaction of ammonia with water:

**NH**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(aq) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) ⇌  NH**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+ **</sup>**(aq) + OH**<sup>**- **</sup>**(aq)**

- The nitrogen in ammonia is covalently bonded to three hydrogen atoms and has one lone pair of electrons causing the ammonia molecule to have a **pyramidal shape**

#### Bonding in ammonia

![Diagram of an NH3 molecule shows a lone pair on nitrogen, covalent bonds with hydrogen, and its pyramidal shape. Labels explain electron pairs.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/8b5f05541dcd-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-shape-and-structure-ammonia.png)

*Ammonia has a pyramidal shape due to its lone pair of electrons*

- The nitrogen atom in ammonia uses its lone pair of electrons to form a dative bond with a proton to form the ammonium ion
- The ammonium ion has a **tetrahedral shape **in which all bonds have the same **length**

#### Bonding in the ammonium ion

![Diagram showing an ammonium ion with a dative covalent bond between nitrogen and a proton, annotated to highlight its tetrahedral shape.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/5a843a21b430-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-shape-and-structure-ammonium.png)

*The tetrahedral shape of the ammonium ion*

### Preparation of ammonia gas from an ammonium salt

- Ammonia gas can be prepared from an ammonium salt and a base in an acid-base reaction:

**2NH**<sub>**4**</sub>**Cl (s) + Ca(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub>** (s) **$\overset{\mathrm{heat}}{\rightarrow}$** CaCl**<sub>**2**</sub>** (s) + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + 2NH**<sub>**3**</sub>** (g)**

- Ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl) and calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub>) are mixed together and then heated
- NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> acts as an **acid **(proton donor) and OH<sup>-</sup> acts as a **base **(proton acceptor)
- The same acid-base reaction (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>-</sup> → NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O) is the basis of the test for ammonium ions: an **unknown solution **is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide
- If the unknown solution contains ammonium ions, the hydroxide ions react with them to form ammonia gas
- This ammonia gas will turn damp red litmus paper blue

#### Producing and testing for ammonia

![Diagram showing ammonia gas production: Ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide are heated; gas travels through a column with calcium oxide, turning litmus paper blue.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/9cb12f645996-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-preparation-of-ammonia-gas.png)

*The diagram shows the apparatus set up for the preparation of ammonia gas from an ammonium salt and calcium hydroxide*

title: Nitrogen Oxides
bodyMd:
# Nitrogen Oxides

## Oxides of Nitrogen

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_WXp9yV6RjmGqJnn3`

## Oxides of Nitrogen

### Natural occurrence of nitrogen oxides

- Due to its lack of reactivity, only under extreme conditions will nitrogen react with oxygen to form **gaseous nitrogen oxides**
- An example of these extreme conditions is **lightning **which can trigger the formation of nitrogen(II) and nitrogen(IV) oxides (NO and NO<sub>2</sub> respectively)
- The chemical equations for these reactions are:

**N**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) → 2NO (g)**

**N**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + 2O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) → 2NO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**

### Man-made occurrence of nitrogen oxides

- In the engine of a car, a mixture of air and fuel is compressed and ignited by a spark
- Air consists of 78% of nitrogen and 21% of oxygen
- Under the high pressure and temperature inside a car engine, nitrogen can react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides
- These nitrogen oxides are released into the **atmosphere **through the car’s **exhaust** **fumes**

### Catalytic removal of nitrogen oxides

- The nitrogen oxides released through cars’ exhaust fumes **pollute **the atmosphere
- Many car exhaust systems are therefore fitted with **catalytic converters **to reduce the **pollutants **from motor vehicles
- The nitrogen oxides are **reduced** on the surface of the **hot catalyst **(eg. platinum) to form the unreactive and harmless nitrogen gas which is then released from the vehicle’s exhaust pipe into the atmosphere
- The chemical reaction for the reduction of nitrogen oxide to nitrogen gas by the catalyst is as follows:

**2CO (g) + 2NO (g) → 2CO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + N**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**

#### Catalytic converters

![Diagram of a car's catalytic converter showing nitrogen oxides converted into nitrogen and carbon dioxide before being released as exhaust gases.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/340786310299-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-catalytic-converters.png)

*Catalytic converters help reduce the pollutant emissions from motor vehicles*

## Oxides of Nitrogen & Photochemical Smog

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_MMZw9fX88jdkvjNh`

## Oxides of Nitrogen & Photochemical Smog

- Nitrogen oxides are examples of **primary pollutants **because they are given off **directly **into the air from the source of pollution

  - Examples of pollution sources are car exhausts and power plants
- Nitrogen oxides are extra dangerous as they can react with substances in the air to make **secondary pollutants**

  - These are pollutants that are not given off directly into the air from human activity
- Exhaust fumes contain another primary pollutant called **volatile organic compound** (**VOCs**)

  - These are unburnt hydrocarbons from fuel and their oxidised products
- VOCs react with nitrogen oxides in air to form **peroxyacetyl** **nitrate** (**PAN**, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>)
- Sunlight provides the energy needed to start off the reactions of VOCs and nitrogen oxides in air, so they are also called **photochemical reactions**
- PAN is one of the harmful pollutants found in **photochemical smog**
- ‘Smog’ is derived from ‘smoke’ and ‘fog’
- PAN affects the lungs and eyes and in high concentrations plant-life

#### Primary & secondary pollutant types & their pollution source summary

- Primary pollutant types

  - Nitrogen oxides (NO / NO<sub>2</sub>)
  
    - Lightning, car exhausts power plants
  - Volatile organic compounds (VOCs)
  
    - Unburnt hydrocarbons from fuel and their oxidised products in exhaust fumes
- Secondary pollutant type

  - Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN, CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>)
  - Photochemical reaction between nitrogen oxides and VOCs

#### The formation of peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN)

![Diagram showing how car exhausts emit VOCs and nitrogen oxides, which react in sunlight to form photochemical smog, including PAN, harming health and nature.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/882feee386b1-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-photochemical-reaction.png)

*The diagram shows the formation of PAN from the photochemical reaction between VOCs and nitrogen oxide*

## Oxides of Nitrogen & Acid Rain

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_v2jg9zFZQVxnN3S7`

## Oxides of Nitrogen & Acid Rain

### Formation of acid rain by nitrogen oxides

- As mentioned earlier, lightning strikes trigger the formation of nitrogen(II) and nitrogen (IV) oxides in air:

**2NO (g) + O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) ⇌ 2NO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**

- The air also contains oxygen and tiny droplets of water that make up clouds
- The nitrogen(IV) oxide (NO<sub>2</sub>) dissolves and reacts in water with oxygen as follows:

**4NO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(aq) + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) + O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) → 4HNO**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(aq)**

- When the clouds rise, the temperature decreases, and the droplets get larger
- When the droplet containing dilute nitric acid are heavy enough, they will fall down as **acid rain**

#### Forming acid rain

![Diagram showing the chemical process of acid rain formation, triggered by lightning creating nitrogen oxides, leading to nitric acid in clouds.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/a8146cb01710-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-acid-rain-formation.png)

*The diagram shows the formation of acid rain by the oxidation of nitrogen(IV) oxide*

### Nitrogen oxide as a catalyst

- Acid rain also contains **dilute sulfuric acid** (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>)
- Sulfur(IV) oxide (SO<sub>2</sub>) is another pollutant found in the atmosphere
- When SO<sub>2</sub> is oxidised, it forms SO<sub>3</sub> which reacts with rainwater to form dilute sulfuric acid as follows:

**SO**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(g) + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O (l) → H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4 **</sub>**(aq)**

- Nitrogen oxides can **directly **cause acid rain but can also act as **catalysts **in the formation of acid rain
- NO<sub>2</sub> catalyses the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> to SO<sub>3</sub>:

**NO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) + SO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) → SO**<sub>**3 **</sub>**(g) + NO (g)**

- The formed NO gets oxidised to regenerate NO<sub>2</sub>:

**NO (g) + ½ O**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g) → NO**<sub>**2 **</sub>**(g)**

- The regenerated NO<sub>2</sub> molecule can get again oxidise another SO<sub>2</sub> molecule to SO<sub>3</sub> which will react with rainwater to form H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

#### Forming sulfuric acid

![NO2 oxidises SO2 to SO3 and is reduced to NO; NO is re-oxidised by half an O2 to regenerate NO2; SO3 then reacts with H2O to produce H2SO4 (sulfuric acid).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/d511c211f533-2-4-nitrogen-sulfur-formation-of-dilute-sulfuric.png)

*The formation of dilute sulfuric acid is catalysed by the nitrogen oxides*

# Functional Groups & their Formulae

## Functional Groups of Organic Compounds

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_fcDYWx3VbRymtyBX`

## Functional Groups of Organic Compounds

- Functional groups determine the physical and chemical properties of molecules
- The table below shows a summary of common functional groups found in compounds
- R is any other atom or group of atoms (except for hydrogen)

#### Functional groups found in compounds table

![An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry Functional Groups, downloadable AS & A Level Chemistry revision notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/20e04e739203-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

## Formulae of Organic Compounds

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_k7Xhrz8Mdj3G3s46`

## Formulae of Organic Compounds

- The **general formula **is a formula that represents a **homologous series** of compounds using letters and numbers

  - Eg. the general formula of alkanes is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>
  - A homologous series is a group of organic compounds that have the same functional group, the same general formula and similar chemical properties
- The **structural formula **is a formula that shows how the atoms are bonded to each carbon atom in a molecule
- The **displayed formula **is a 2D representation of an organic molecule showing **all** its atoms (by their **symbols**) and their bonds (by single, double or triple bonds)
- The **skeletal formula** is a simplified displayed formula with all the carbon and hydrogen (C-H) bonds removed

title: Hydrocarbons & Alkanes
bodyMd:
# Hydrocarbons & Alkanes

## Hydrocarbons

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_jptnPNnPshVwycwD`

## Hydrocarbons

- **Organic chemistry** is the chemistry of carbon compounds
- Carbon forms a vast number of compounds because it can form strong covalent bonds with itself
- This enables it to form long chains of carbon atoms, branched chains or cycles, and hence an almost infinite variety of carbon compounds are known
- Carbon always forms four covalent bonds which can be single, double or triple bonds

#### Examples of carbon structures

![Three chemical structures: linear chain of carbon atoms, branched carbon chain, and a hexagonal ring of carbon atoms, each with attached hydrogen atoms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/b18d5a98e992-10-1-1-catenation-in-carbon-1.png)

*There is an almost infinite variety of chains, branches and rings able to form*

- A **functional group** is a specific atom or group of atoms which confer certain physical and chemical properties onto the molecule
- Organic molecules are classified by the dominant **functional group** on the molecule
- Organic compounds with the same functional group, but with each successive member different by CH<sub>2</sub> are called a **homologous series**

  - Every time a carbon atom is added to the chain, two hydrogen atoms are also added, which is why the successive members differ by CH<sub>2</sub>

- Hydrocarbons are compounds that are made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms **ONLY**

#### Examples of hydrocarbons

![Diagram showing structures of methane, ethane, propane, and butane as hydrocarbons. Ethanol is crossed out as it contains oxygen, not a hydrocarbon.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/614aeb6a896c-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Ethanol is NOT a hydrocarbon as the molecule also contains an oxygen atom and is not solely made up of carbon and hydrogen*

> **Exam Hint**
> You must state that hydrocarbons are ‘**only’** made up of C and H atoms if defining this term in an exam

## Alkanes

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_Bk6CctHBVZ7t2gBH`

## Alkanes

- A **functional group **is an atom or a group of atoms in an organic molecule, which determines the physical and chemical properties of the molecule
- **Alkanes **are the simplest hydrocarbons with no functional group
- They are made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms bonded to each other with single covalent bonds

#### Different types of alkanes

![Diagram showing three alkane types: linear (two bonded carbons), branched (three bonded carbons in a T-shape), and cyclic (triangle of three carbons).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/2524cb1552ba-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Alkanes are compounds made up of carbon and hydrogen atoms only and contain no functional group*

#### Homologous series of alkanes table

| **Name of alkane** | **Number of carbons** | **Chemical formula** | **Boiling point in °C** | **State at room temp** | **Melting point in °C** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Methane | 1 | CH<sub>4</sub> | -161 | gas | -182 |
| Ethane | 2 | C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> | -88 | gas | -183 |
| Propane | 3 | C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> | -42 | gas | -188 |
| Butane | 4 | C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> | -0.5 | gas | -138 |
| Pentane | 5 | C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> | 36 | liquid | -130 |

## Molecular & Empirical Formulae of Organic Compounds

# Naming of Organic Compounds ## Nomenclature of Aliphatic Compounds > **Spec point** — `spcpt_nf3jtTMfZNRyHcQF` ## Nomenclature of Aliphatic Compounds - **Systematic nomenclature **can be used to name organic compounds and therefore make it easier to refer to them - The **alkanes** provide the basis of the naming system and the **stem** of each name indicates how many carbon atoms are in the **longest chain **in one molecule of the compound #### Nomenclature of organic compounds table | **Number of C atoms** | **Molecular formula of straight-chain alkane** | **Name of alkane** | **Stem used in naming** | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | CH4 | methane | meth- | | 2 | C2H6 | ethane | eth- | | 3 | C3H8 | propane | prop- | | 4 | C4H10 | butane | but- | | 5 | C5H12 | pentane | pent- | | 6 | C6H14 | hexane | hex- | | 7 | C7H16 | heptane | hept- | | 8 | C8H18 | octane | oct- | | 9 | C9H20 | nonane | non- | | 10 | C10H22 | decane | dec- | ### Side chains - When naming compounds with side chains or functional groups, number the carbon atoms in the longest chain, starting from the end that gives the lowest possible numbers to the substituents - In structural formulas, a side chain is often shown in brackets. - E.g. CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 - Side chains are named by changing the **-ane** ending of the parent alkane to** -yl** - These groups are known as alkyl groups #### Naming organic compounds with one alkyl side chain ![Displayed formula of 3-methylhexane with the carbon chain numbered from each end; numbering from the left gives the lowest number, 3, for the methyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/3056cfe20685-31132-naming-organic-compounds-with-one-alkyl-si.png) *The longest chain provides the main name and the side chain is shown as a numbered alkyl prefix* - If there are more than one of the same alkyl side chain or functional groups, **di-** (for two), **tri-** (for three) or **tetra-** (for four) is added in front of its name - The adjacent **numbers **have a comma between them - **Numbers **are separated from **words **by a hyphen #### Naming organic compounds with multiple, identical side chains ![Displayed formula of 3,3,4-trimethylhexane with the longest chain numbered 1 to 6, two methyl groups on carbon 3 and one on carbon 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/032d12bf16b6-38749-naming-organic-compounds-with-multiple-ide.png) *The longest chain still provides the main name and the side chains are shown as numbered alkyl prefixes* - If there is more than one type of alkyl side chain, the same numbering system applies but the different side chains are listed in alphabetic order #### Naming organic compounds with multiple, different side chains ![Displayed formula of 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane with the longest chain numbered 1 to 6, a methyl group on carbon 2 and an ethyl group on carbon 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/0cc1b2124215-61901-naming-organic-compounds-with-multiple-dif.png) *The longest chain still provides the main name and the side chains are still shown as numbered alkyl prefixes but in alphabetical order* #### Functional groups & their nomenclature table | **Class** | **Systematic prefix–**

# Characteristic Organic Reactions

## Definitions in Organic Chemistry

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_jWB5gK4XNw8yxZ9R`

## Definitions & Terminology in Organic Chemistry

### Homologous series

- A homologous series is a group of organic compounds that have the same functional group, the same general formula and similar chemical properties

#### The homologous series of alcohols

![Structural formulas of ethanol and propanol, both with alcohol groups (-OH), similar formula (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH), and chemical reactivity.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/0c68d5b73287-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Ethanol and propanol belong to the same homologous series*

### Saturated & unsaturated hydrocarbons

- **Saturated **hydrocarbons are hydrocarbons which contain single bonds only resulting in the maximum number of hydrogen atoms in the molecule
- **Unsaturated **hydrocarbons are hydrocarbons which contain carbon-carbon **double** or **triple** bonds

#### Comparing the alkane and alkene homologous series

![Diagrams of butane and butene; butane is a saturated hydrocarbon with single C-H bonds, butene is unsaturated with a double bond. Descriptions included.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/8b7dd6687d36-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*The diagram shows saturated hydrocarbons which contain single bonds only and unsaturated hydrocarbons which contain double/triple bonds as well*

### Homolytic & heterolytic fission

- **Homolytic fission **is breaking a covalent bond in such a way that each atom takes an electron from the bond to form two radicals
- **Heterolytic fission **is breaking a covalent bond in such a way that the more electronegative atom takes both the electrons from the bond to form a negative ion and leaves behind a positive ion

#### Examples of homolytic & heterolytic fission

![Diagram explaining heterolytic and homolytic fission of covalent bonds, showing electron distribution between atoms X and Y in different scenarios.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/b878d91b7ccf-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*In heterolytic fission, the most electronegative atom takes both electrons in the covalent bond. While in homolytic fission, each atom takes one electron from the covalent bond*

### Radical chain reactions

- A **free radical **is a species with one (or more than one) unpaired electrons

#### Free radicals

![Diagram showing a stable atom becoming a free radical by removing an electron, resulting in one unpaired electron and instability.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/e02f217f7b99-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*The diagram shows a free radical which has one unpaired electron*

- A **free radical reaction **is a reaction involving free radicals and is a three-step reaction:

  - **Initiation **is the first step and involves breaking a covalent bond using energy from ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun to form two free radicals
  - The **propagation **step is the second step in which a radical formed in initiation attacks a reactant molecule to form a new radical (one radical is used up and one is made, so the number of radicals does not increase)
  
    - These in turn can again attack other molecules to form more free radicals and so on
  - In the **termination **step, two free radicals react together to form a product molecule

#### The steps of a free radical reaction mechanism

![Diagram of free radical reactions: initiation, propagation, and termination, showing how radicals are generated and collide to form stable molecules.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/c041c8910d10-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*The main steps of a free radical reaction mechanism are initiation, propagation and termination*

### Nucleophiles & electrophiles

- A **nucleophile** is an electron-rich species that can **donate** a pair of electrons

  - ‘Nucleophile’ means ‘nucleus/positive charge loving’ as nucleophiles are attracted to positively charged species
  - **Nucleophilic **refers to reactions that involve a nucleophile
- An **electrophile **is an electron-deficient species that can **accept **a pair of electrons

  - ‘Electrophile’ means ‘electron/negative charge loving’ as electrophiles are attracted to negatively charged species
  - **Electrophilic** refers to reactions that involve an electrophile

#### Examples of a nucleophile and an electrophile

![Diagram of nucleophile and electrophile interaction. Oxygen donates electrons to hydrogen ion, forming a covalent bond in a water molecule.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/b18017be080f-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*A nucleophile ‘loves’ a positive charge and an electrophile ‘loves’ a negative charge*

### Types of reactions

- An **addition **reaction is an organic reaction in which two (or more) molecules combine to give a **single** **product** with no other products
- A **substitution **reaction is a reaction that involves **replacing** an atom or group of atoms with another atom or group of atoms
- An **elimination **reaction is a reaction in which a small molecule (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl) is **removed** from an organic molecule
- A **hydrolysis **reaction is a reaction in which a compound is **broken** **down** by **water** (it can also refer to the breakdown of a substance by dilute acids or alkalis)
- A **condensation **reaction is a reaction in which two organic molecules join together and in the process **eliminate** small molecules (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl)

#### The different types of reactions in organic chemistry

![Diagram illustrating addition, substitution, and elimination reactions with ethene, halogens, and water. Text explains molecular changes with chemical equations.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/9d2e83560886-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

![Diagram illustrating hydrolysis and condensation reactions. Hydrolysis shows an ester breaking into alcohol and acid; condensation shows alcohol and acid forming an ester.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/fce2d891dfe1-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*It is important to be able to describe and identify the different types of reaction in organic chemistry*

### Oxidation & reduction

- An **oxidation **reaction is a reaction in which oxygen is added, electrons are removed or the oxidation number of a substance is increased

  - In organic chemistry, it often refers to the **addition of oxygen **or removal of hydrogen atoms to a substance
  - In equations for organic redox reactions, the symbol** [O]** can be used to represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent
- A **reduction **reaction is a reaction in which oxygen is removed, electrons are added or the oxidation number of a substance is decreased

  - In organic chemistry, it often refers to the **removal of oxygen **or addition of hydrogen atoms to a substance
  - In equations for organic redox reactions, the symbol** [H] **can be used to represent one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent

#### Examples of oxidation and reduction

![Diagram illustrating oxidation and reduction reactions involving ethanol and ethanal, with accompanying chemical equations and structural formulae.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/54b5efb518a8-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*In organic chemistry oxidation is often the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen atoms and reduction is the gain of hydrogen and loss of oxygen atoms*

title: Terminology Used in Reaction Mechanisms

# Terminology Used in Reaction Mechanisms

## Terminology of Reaction Mechanisms

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_qDgtcCxSVxWwxNfy`

## Terminology Used in Reaction Mechanisms

- In organic reaction mechanisms, **curly** **arrows** represent the movement of **electron** **pairs**
- The arrow begins at a bond or a lone pair of electrons and points to the species that accepts the lone pair of electrons

#### An organic mechanism curly arrow

![Diagram showing electron pair movement from source to destination, represented by a blue arrow connecting two red dashed circles.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/df80d9c6a17c-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Curly arrows show electron pairs moving from the source (eg. a nucleophile) to its destination (eg. an electrophile)*

### Free-radical substitution

- A **free-radical substitution reaction **is a reaction in which halogen atoms substitute for hydrogen atoms in alkanes
- Free radical substitution involves three standard steps:

  - Initiation
  - Propagation
  - Termination

#### Initiation step

- The covalent Cl-Cl bond is broken by energy from the UV light
- Each atom takes **one electron** from the covalent bond
- This produces two radicals in a **homolytic** **fission** reaction

**Cl–Cl → 2Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>

#### Propagation step

- The halogen free radicals are very reactive and will attack the unreactive alkanes
- One of the methane C-H bond breaks homolytically to produce an alkyl radical

**CH**<sub>**4**</sub>** + Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>** → **<sup>**•**</sup>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + HCl**

- The alkyl radical can attack another chlorine molecule to form a halogenoalkane
- This also regenerates the chlorine free radical

<sup>**•**</sup>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>** → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**Cl + Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>** **

- The regenerated chlorine free radical can then repeat the cycle

#### Termination step

- Multiple products are possible, dependent on the radicals involved

  - They are commonly classed as desirable (wanted) and undesirable (unwanted)
- In the single substitution of methane with chlorine:

  - Chloromethane is the desirable (wanted) product:

<sup>**•**</sup>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>** → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**Cl **

- Ethane and chlorine are undesirable (unwanted) products:

<sup>**•**</sup>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** + **<sup>**•**</sup>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** → CH**<sub>**3**</sub>**CH**<sub>**3**</sub>** **

**Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>** + Cl**<sup>**•**</sup>** → Cl**<sub>**2**</sub>

### Electrophilic addition

- An **electrophilic addition **reaction is a reaction in which an electron rich region in a molecule is attacked by an electrophile (a species that likes electrons/negative charge) followed by the addition of a small molecule to give one product only

#### Example of an electrophilic addition reaction to form ethanol from ethene

![Chemical reaction diagram showing electrophilic addition of H+ to ethene, forming ethanol with text boxes explaining the reaction process.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/266a5c2f7c3b-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level.png)

*Curly arrows always move from an area of high electron density to an area of low electron density*

### Nucleophilic substitution

- A **nucleophilic substitution **reaction is a reaction in which an electron-rich nucleophile **displaces** a halogen atom

#### The general nucleophilic substitution reaction mechanism

![Chemical reaction diagram showing nucleophilic substitution: nucleophile Nu⁻ replaces X⁻ in R-CH₂-X, forming R-CH₂-Nu and X⁻ ion.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/78ee394840e9-7-9-1-general-mechanism-nucleoph.png)

*In nucleophilic substitution reaction mechanisms, the nucleophile replaces an atom / group in the target molecule*

- The C-X carbon of the halogenoalkane is electron deficient and has a δ+ charge

  - The halogen atom, X, is more electronegative than the carbon atom which means that it pulls electrons towards itself and is δ–
- The nucleophile has a lone pair of electrons that it can donate to the δ+ carbon atom and form a covalent bond
- This causes the displacement of the halogen atom, X, which leaves as a halide ion, X<sup>–</sup>

  - The displaced halide ion is known as a **leaving group**

### Nucleophilic addition

- A **nucleophilic addition **reaction is a reaction in which a nucleophile (a species that likes a nucleus/positive charge) attacks an electron-deficient region in a molecule followed by the addition of a small molecule to give one product only

#### The general nucleophilic addition reaction mechanism

![Nucleophilic addition mechanism: nucleophile attacks carbonyl carbon, forming alkoxide, then alcohol after protonation from solvent.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/226a16bd5036-7-2-3-nucleophilic-addition-with-ketones.png)

*In nucleophilic addition reaction mechanisms, the nucleophile is added to the target molecule*

title: Hybridisation in Organic Molecules
bodyMd:
# Hybridisation in Organic Molecules

## Hybridised Atoms: Shapes & Bond Angles in Molecules

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_QytGnRrdQn5z8m9n`

## Hybridised Atoms: Shapes & Bond Angles in Molecules

- Each carbon atom has four electrons in its outer shell (**electronic configuration**: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>2</sup>)
- Carbon atoms share these four electrons in four covalent bonds with other atoms to achieve a **full outer shell configuration**
- These electrons are found in orbitals within the respective atoms
- When forming a covalent bond, the orbitals overlap in such a way to form two types of bonds

  - Sigma bonds (σ)
  - Pi bonds (π)

### Hybridisation: sp<sup>3</sup>

- The electron pair in a σ bond is found in a region of space between the nuclei of the two atoms that are sharing the electrons
- The **electrostatic** **attraction** between the **electrons** (negatively charged) and the two **nuclei** (positively charged) holds the two atoms together
- Carbon atoms that form four σ bonds are said to be **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> **hybridised**
- The four pairs of electrons around each carbon repel each other forcing the molecule to adopt a configuration in which the bonding pairs of electrons are as far away from each other as possible

  - The molecule adopts a **tetrahedral** arrangement with bond angles of **109.5 **<sup>**o**</sup>

#### Bonding in ethane

![Diagram of an ethane molecule with two carbon atoms bonded and six hydrogen atoms, showing tetrahedral geometry and 3D bond angles.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/fa783a845ee7-43059-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2020123-1-a.png)

*The diagram shows a molecule of ethane in which each carbon atom forms four σ bonds to adopt a tetrahedral configuration and minimise the repulsion between the bonding pairs of electrons*

### Hybridisation: sp<sup>2</sup>

- When carbon atoms use only three of their electron pairs to form σ bonds, they are said to be **sp**<sup>**2**</sup> **hybridised**

  - Each carbon atom will have a p orbital which contains **one** spare electron
- When the p orbitals of two carbon atoms overlap with each other, a π bond is formed (the π bond contains two electrons)
- The two orbitals that form the π bond lie above and below the plane of the two carbon atoms to maximise bond overlap
- The three bonding pairs of electrons are in the plane of the molecule and repel each other
- The molecule adopts a **planar **arrangement with bond angles of **120 **<sup>**o**</sup>

#### Bonding in ethene

![Diagram showing ethene's hybridisation with p and s orbitals forming a sigma bond and pi bond, displaying its planar structure with 120° angles.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/39b1345fdeb8-54968-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2020123-1-a.png)

*The overlap of the two p orbitals results in the formation of a π bond in ethene (sp2 hybridised molecule) in which the bonding pair of electrons repel each other to force the molecule into a planar configuration with bond angles of 120o*

### Hybridisation: sp

- Carbon atoms can also use only two of their electron pairs to form σ bonds, in which case the carbon atoms are said to be **sp hybridised**

  - Each carbon atom will have **two** p orbitals with **one **spare electron each
- When the four p orbitals of the carbon atoms overlap with each other, **two** π bonds are formed (each π bond contains two electrons)
- The two orbitals that form the π bond lie above and below the plane of the carbon atoms
- The two orbitals of the **other **π bond lie in front and behind the plane of the atoms

  - This maximises the overlap of the four p orbitals
- The molecule adopts a **linear **arrangement with bond angles **180 **<sup>**o**</sup>

#### Bonding in ethyne

![Diagram of ethyne molecule showing orbital hybridisation. S and P orbitals form σ and π bonds. Bond angle is 180 degrees between hydrogen and carbon.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/a694536d00da-2896-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2020123-1-an.png)

*The overlap of the p orbitals results in the formation of two π bonds in ethyne (sp hybridised molecule) which adopts a linear arrangement with bond angles of 180o*

> **Exam Hint**
> A **double** **bond** is a combination of a σ and π bond and a **triple** **bond** is a combination of one σ and two π bonds
> 
> The strength of the bonds increases as follows: **single < double < triple bond**
> 
> This is due to the increased electron density around the C-C atom, making the bond stronger and more difficult to break.

## Hybridised Atoms: σ & π Bonds in Molecules

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_qzx4VbjHZKNywYNz`

## Hybridised Atoms: σ and π Bonds in Molecules

### σ bonds

- Sigma bonds are formed from the end-on overlap of atomic orbitals

  - S orbitals overlap this way as well as p orbitals

#### Forming sigma bonds

![Diagram illustrating sigma bond formation from orbital overlap: s-s, p-s, and p-p, with arrows indicating bond formation.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/c14616319881-48415-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2020123-1-a.png)

*Sigma bonds can be formed from the end-on overlap of s or p orbitals*

- The electron density in a σ bond is **symmetrical** about a line joining the nuclei of the atoms forming the bond

  - The pair of electrons is found between the nuclei of the two atoms
  - The electrostatic attraction between the electrons and nuclei bonds the atoms to each other

#### The arrangement of the σ bond in sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup> and sp hybridised carbon atoms

![Diagram showing sigma bonds in sp3, sp2, and sp hybridised molecules, illustrating carbon-hydrogen and carbon-carbon bonding with labelled orbitals.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/9ebc81753988-35951-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021013-1-a.png)

*The σ orbitals are formed from the end-on overlap of the atomic orbitals resulting in symmetrical electron density on the atoms*

### π bonds

- Pi (π) bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of p orbitals
- The two lobes that make up the π bond lie above and below the plane of the atoms

  - This maximises the overlap of the p orbitals

#### Forming pi bonds

![Diagram showing the formation of π bonds from the overlap of p-orbitals, with arrows indicating the process and resulting π bonds highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/484597f5e8c4-22668-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2020123-1-a.png)

*π bonds can be formed from the sideways overlap of p orbitals*

- In triple bonds, there is an additional overlap of p orbital
- The two lobes of the π bond lie in front of and behind the plane of the atoms in the molecule

  - This maximises the overlap of the p orbitals

#### The arrangement of the π bond in sp<sup>2</sup> and sp hybridised carbon atoms

![Diagram showing pi bonds in sp2 and sp hybridised molecules, with overlapping lobes and labelled pi bonds for carbon-carbon interactions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/fb0657902a34-63448-httpscdn-savemyexams-comuploads2021013-1-a.png)

*The π bonds are formed from the sideway overlap of the atomic orbitals*

> **Exam Hint**
> π bonds are drawn as two electron clouds, one arising from each lobe of the p orbitals
> 
> The two clouds of electrons in a π bond represent **one **bond consisting of **two **electrons (one from each orbital)

# Planarity of Organic Molecules

## Planar Molecules

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_Bb7Zq92CG2N8Mfgn`

## Planar Molecules

- Planar molecules have all their atoms in the same plane

  - E.g. linear, bent, trigonal planar and square planar

#### Examples of planar molecules

![Diagram of molecular shapes: linear, non-linear (bent), trigonal planar, and square planar, showing bond angles of 180°, 104.5°, 120°, and 90°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/bf4582cabc57-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*The diagram shows molecules which have all their atoms in the same plane with their name and the associated bond angle*

- The presence of an sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon can force the molecule to adopt a planar configuration **(trigonal planar**)
- The 3 σ bonds position themselves in a trigonal planar position so that the bonding pair of electrons are as far away from each other and therefore minimise the repulsion between them

#### The planarity of ethene

![Diagram of ethene showing structural formula and ball-and-stick model, illustrating trigonal planar geometry of carbon atoms and hydrogen bonds.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/25ca3522aa7c-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Ethene is a planar molecule with two trigonal planar centres around the carbon atoms*

#### The planarity of propene

![Structural diagrams of propene, showing molecular geometry: tetrahedral and trigonal planar centres, with hydrogen and carbon atoms labelled.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/e14534fbb53b-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistry-pl.png)

*Propene has two trigonal planar centres around the carbon-carbon double bond and one tetrahedral centre*

- The presence of an sp hybridised carbon can also force the molecule to adopt a planar configuration (**linear**)
- The 2 σ bonds position themselves in a linear position to minimise the repulsion between the bonding pairs of electrons

#### The planarity of ethyne

![Diagram of ethyne molecule, showing its linear structure. Includes chemical formula HC≡CH, with hydrogen and carbon atoms in blue and pink circles.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/27b0bd6a37da-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Ethyne is a planar molecule with one planar centre: the molecule is linear*

#### The planarity of propyne

![Propyne, HC≡CCH3, shown as a structural formula and a ball-and-stick model: the three carbons and the first hydrogen lie on a straight line, and the CH3 group is a tetrahedral centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/02eb78a3187f-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Propyne has one planar centre around the carbon-carbon triple bond (linear) and one tetrahedral centre*

title: Chirality
bodyMd:
# Chirality

## Chirality & Enantiomers

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_X7vDgdxQs3VpCRb6`

## Chirality & Enantiomers

### Chiral centres in non-cyclic molecules

- A **chiral** **centre** in a molecule is a carbon atom that has four different atoms or groups of atoms attached
- This gives rise to two optical isomers which are also called **enantiomers**
- The enantiomers are **mirror images **of each other and cannot be superimposed

#### Chiral centres in non-cyclic molecules

![Diagram showing a chiral centre with a carbon atom bonded to H, OH, CH₃, and Br groups, illustrating two non-superimposable enantiomers.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/ea5e99fa7bcd-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*The presence of the chiral centre in the molecule allows two enantiomers to exist which are stereoisomers as the molecules have the same atoms bonded to each other, but they are differently arranged in space*

- When the molecule contains more than one chiral centre (asymmetric carbon) more than two optical isomers will be formed

  - If there are two chiral centres, each chiral centre can have two arrangements in space (mirror-image forms)
  - There are **four** possible optical isomers

#### Molecules with multiple chiral centres

![Diagram showing a molecule with two chiral centres, leading to four optical isomers labelled 1 to 4, each with different hydroxyl and hydrogen arrangements.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/712673b8a3a4-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*Each chiral centre gives rise to two optical isomers; therefore, the molecule has a total of four optical isomers*

### Chiral centres in cyclic molecules

- To determine the chiral centre in a cyclic molecule, the carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups of atoms should be found

  - E.g. 2-aminocyclohexanol has two chiral centres so it can form four optical isomers

#### Chiral centres in cyclic molecules

![Diagram showing two chiral centres on a carbon ring with attached groups: HO, NH₂ and hydrogen. Descriptions of clockwise and anti-clockwise bonding.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/32e32b2c8625-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

*To decide where the chiral centres are in a cyclic molecule, the carbon atoms bonded to four different atoms or atom groups should be found*

> **Exam Hint**
> Use a **molecular modelling kit** and make the models of enantiomers to help you understand that the two molecules are non-superimposable and therefore non-identical

## Identifying Chirality & Geometrical Isomerism

> **Spec point** — `spcpt_pzjCCN5WFBRwTq6P`

## Identifying Chirality & Geometrical Isomerism

#### Identify chirality

- Identifying **chiral** **centres** in cyclic and non-cyclic compounds is very straightforward as it is the carbon with four different atoms or atom groups in a molecule
- This gives rise to **two** optical isomers
- When more than two chiral centres are present, more than two optical isomers exist

  - The maximum number of stereoisomers that a molecule can have is 2<sup>n</sup>, where n is the number of chiral centres
- So, a molecule with **three** chiral centres will have 2<sup>3</sup> = **eight **optical isomers
- A molecule containing chiral centres is called a **chiral molecule**

### Identifying geometrical isomers

- Molecules with restricted rotation about the C-C bond can have geometrical isomers, provided each of the two carbons joined by that bond (the C=C carbons, or two ring carbons) carries two different groups
- This includes unsaturated and cyclic compounds

  - E.g. alkenes (such as but-2-ene) and substituted rings (such as 1,2-dichlorocyclopentane)
- When the groups are positioned on the same side of the C-C double bond, the compound is a **cis **isomer
- When the groups are positioned on opposite sides of the C-C double bond the compound is a **trans **isomer

> **Worked Example**
> **Drawing optical isomers**
>

>

> 
> **Answers:**
> 
> ![Three chemical reactions showing chiral centres; each reaction splits into two enantiomers, marked and highlighted in coloured circles.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/e318174f559d-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)

Shows structural formulas and names: cis/trans-2-butene and cis/trans-1,2-dichlorocyclopentane.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-RevisionNotes/cie-as-chemistry-25/assets/2aefd4b85bf2-3-1-an-introduction-to-as-level-organic-chemistr.png)
